newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: RUGBY UNION-LIONS' TOURS TO REMAIN INFREQUENT.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-LIONS' TOURS TO REMAIN INFREQUENT.

text.p: Despite the resounding success of the 1997 tour of South Africa, future British Lions tours will take place only once every four years, chairman of the Four Home Unions tours committee Ray Williams said on Sunday.
While complimenting Martin Johnson's class of 1997 on their 2-1 series victory over South Africa, Williams warned against allowing rugby union tradition to be cheapened by frequency of matches.
"I'm totally opposed to Louis Luyt's innuendo that the Lions should tour more often. That's just pie in the sky and it would never happen," Williams said.
"The Lions will tour once every four years, bracketed between each World Cup, and no more than that. There is a danger here that we could kill the goose that laid the golden egg.

"The Lions will never play a one-off test at home. There would have to be a structured season allowing the players to get together and prepare well in advance of any test. The clubs, who own the players, would be reluctant to release them on a regular basis.

"Since the game has gone professional, we have seen that regularity of matches can become stale. Within the southern hemisphere South Africa and New Zealand are now playing each other several times each season and this has taken away the magic of a long-established tradition."

Williams cited the example of Wales staging matches in Cardiff last year against both Australia and world champions South Africa: "Two great rugby powers and yet we couldn't fill the Cardiff Arms Park on either occasion," he said.
But inspirational Lions coach Ian McGeechan believes the British Lions should play more often.
"We have to establish a level above the Five Nations and I would like to see the Lions playing at home as part of a structured season," he said.
"We can't accept the Five Nations as the acceptable level of competition in the northern hemisphere. There has to be something higher."
Lions manager Fran Cotton said there was still a gap in northern hemisphere rugby for a Super 12-style competition in Europe.
"Northern hemisphere rugby still lags three to four years behind rugby in the southern hemisphere and we should be looking to develop the Five Nations," Cotton said.

"But I don't think the establishment of the Tri-Nations competition (involving South Africa, New Zealand and Australia) puts the northern hemisphere at a disadvantage. New Zealand coach John Hart wanted England and France to join it but it would be absolute lunacy for us to break away from the Five Nations.

"A decision needs to be taken between either the provincial or the club route. South Africa has decided to take the regional route as the best one for the development of their rugby and this is a matter we must address with some urgency."
